echoes.note: Jeremiah's oracle that God will punish all who are "circumcised yet uncircumcised"—Israel being uncircumcised in heart—anticipates Paul's devaluing of fleshly circumcision in favor of inward transformation (vv.12-15). Volume is moderate; the prophetic relativizing of physical circumcision strongly coheres with Paul's argument.

echoes.text: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.
echoes.note: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart" supplies the Torah's own move from fleshly to inward circumcision, the trajectory Paul completes with "new creation" (v.15). Coherence is high and the motif recurs (Deut 30:6); offered as a corroborating echo of the heart-circumcision tradition.

pericopes.text: As many as walk by this rule, peace and mercy be on them, and on God’s Israel. From now on, let no one cause me any trouble, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

echoes.text: But as for those who turn aside to their crooked ways, Yahweh will lead them away with the workers of iniquity. Peace be on Israel.
echoes.note: "Peace... on God's Israel" (v.16) echoes the psalm's closing benediction "Peace be upon Israel," a liturgical blessing Paul redirects to those who walk by the rule of new creation. Volume and the formulaic shape (peace-upon-Israel) are high; coherence with a closing benediction is exact.

echoes.text: Yes, may you see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel.
echoes.note: Psalm 128:6 likewise ends "Peace be upon Israel," reinforcing v.16 as a deliberate echo of the Psalter's pilgrimage benediction. Recurrence of the exact phrase across Pss 125 and 128 strengthens availability; Paul invokes the blessing while redefining its recipients.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The Aaronic benediction—"the LORD... give you peace"—is the liturgical fountainhead for pronouncing peace and mercy upon Israel (v.16). Volume of the peace-blessing motif is high though the verbal contact is thematic; coherence with a closing apostolic blessing is strong.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark on the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry over all the abominations that are done in its midst. To the others he said in my hearing, Go through the city after him, and strike: don’t let your eye spare, neither have pity; kill utterly the old man, the young man and the virgin, and little children and women; but don’t come near any man on whom is […]
echoes.note: "I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body" (v.17) evokes the protective mark (taw) set on the foreheads of the faithful who are spared the slaughter. The marking that distinguishes God's own coheres with Paul's stigmata as the true seal over against circumcision; verbal contact is figural but apt.

echoes.text: One will say, ‘I am Yahweh’s;’ and another will be called by the name of Jacob; and another will write with his hand ‘to Yahweh,’ and honor the name of Israel.”
echoes.note: Isaiah's image of one who "writes on his hand, 'The LORD's,'" marking belonging to God, parallels Paul's bodily "marks of Jesus" (v.17) as a sign of ownership. Coherence with the slave-brand/belonging motif is good; volume is moderate and the link is figural.

echoes.text: “You shall make a plate of pure gold, and engrave on it, like the engravings of a signet, ‘HOLY TO YAHWEH.’ You shall put it on a lace of blue, and it shall be on the sash; on the front of the sash it shall be. It shall be on Aaron’s forehead, and Aaron shall bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall make holy in all their holy gifts; and it shall be always on his forehead, that they may be accepted before Yahweh.
echoes.note: The high-priestly gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD" worn on the body has been proposed as background for Paul's engraved marks of Jesus (v.17). The cultic-engraving association is suggestive but verbally remote; offered as a contested, low-volume echo.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor tattoo any marks on you. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The Torah's prohibition of cutting marks in the flesh forms an ironic backdrop to Paul's embrace of the "marks of Jesus" (v.17) as honorable wounds. The connection is conceptual rather than citational and runs by contrast; marked contested.
